Some notches have a bear whose swipe is telegraphed 0.8 s ahead (it leans and its shadow darkens), so you leap between swipes or pick another notch. Eagle shadows circle and dive at a marked spot. Being caught costs one of 3 scales. Five rival salmon are visible and contestable: they swim seeded lines with their own rhythm skill and leap odds, a rival waiting in a notch blocks it until it leaps, and in the foam pools you can bump them aside (and be bumped) for a better launch spot. A run is 3 stages of about 90 s each (lower river, gorge, mountain stream), placed at each spawning pool. The run ends after stage 3 (reason 'win') or when all 3 scales are lost (reason 'lose'). Score = placement points + time + shrimp.
games.controls: Two thumbs: tap the left or right half to stroke and turn toward that side, alternate to swim straight, and hold to charge a leap at a waterfall. Keyboard: Left/Right arrows to stroke, Space to charge and leap.
games.progression: Stages within a run get faster flow, taller falls, more bears and tighter rhythm windows. Once the 3-stage run is done, 'next year's run' continues with harder rules and a year counter for endless play. Daily seeded river. Skins unlock (bright breeding colours, a silver ocean fish, a hooked-jaw male). Choosing between eddy rest stops and a strong stroke rhythm, plus reading which notch to leap, keeps decisions alive throughout.
games.art: A glacier-fed river in late summer, seen from above. Milky jade water (#5fb3a8 in the shallows to #2a6a6e in the channel) with a subtle shimmer of sun flecks riding the current (no caustic network) and foam streak particles following the flow field. Rounded grey granite boulders (#8b8f94) with lichen, banks of magenta fireweed (#d23f8a) and dark spruce (#1f3b30), and floating spruce needles and fireweed petals. Salmon are sinuous 6-segment bodies that sway with each stroke: red #d9473b flanks, olive-green heads, silver bellies, dark spots. Bears are big brown top-down silhouettes standing in the falls, with fur-edge strokes and pale claws. Waterfalls are stepped white sheets with mist plumes and a faint rainbow. HUD styled as river stones and slate: a vertical river line on the left with fish icons for every racer, stamina as scale-shaped pips, the rhythm shown as glowing gill marks. Shell theme: river-stone slate panels with fireweed corners and a pebble button.
games.audio: Folk-acoustic synth at 92 bpm in a major pentatonic: a plucked-string patch, soft hand drum, low drone. Near falls the drum pattern doubles. Sound effects: tail stroke (filtered noise slap, panned left or right, pitch alternating), rhythm streak (rising chime), leap charge (rising whoosh), clean leap (big splash plus bell), failed leap (tumble splash), bear swipe (low FM growl plus whoosh), eagle cry (sine sweep), shrimp gulp (pop).
juice: Each stroke flicks a splash of droplets off the side you tapped
At max rhythm the fish leaves a glowing silver wake
A leap goes into slow motion over the lip with the camera pulling back through the spray
A bear swipe that misses whiffs its claws and throws a sheet of spray
An eagle's shadow grows on the water before it dives
Arriving at the spawning pool bursts confetti of fireweed petals
games.teach: The run opens in a calm pool with almost no current. Ghost thumbs tap left and right in rhythm while ripples mark each side. The first waterfall is a single low notch with a ghost 'hold then release'. Track tutorial_complete after the first successful leap.
games.scenes: art: a salmon mid-leap over a waterfall while a bear's paw swipes, spray and a rainbow, rival fish jostling in the foam pool below, fireweed on the banks, no HUD. shot1: the lower-river start with a school of six salmon and the stone HUD. shot2: the gorge with eddies behind rocks, an eagle shadow and the rhythm meter at max.
games.feasibility: Low to medium risk. The flow field is an analytic function of distance from the river spline plus local vortex terms for each rock, with no fluid simulation. The fish is velocity plus heading. Leaps are 2.5D (sprite scale and a separate shadow). Rivals follow the centreline with seeded offsets and rhythm skill, and share the player's circle collisions, so bumps and notch blocking are real. The river is drawn in chunks baked offscreen, with the sun-fleck shimmer as one scrolling tile. Test hook ?debug exposes window.__game { start(seed, stage), stroke('L'|'R'), leap(power), autoSwim(true), loseScale(), endRun(), state() } so Playwright can swim a stage and force a loss.

games.title: Lumen Court
games.pitch: Turn brass mirrors to cross coloured light. Light each crystal its exact hue.
games.hook: Tap a mirror and a red ray swings across the moonlit courtyard. Cross it with green and the crystal blooms yellow: colour mixing you see and hear instantly.
games.loop: A 7x9 grid. Lens emitters in the walls (brass lenses that focus moonlight through coloured glass) fire red, green or blue beams. Pieces: brass mirrors (/ or \, tap to rotate 90 degrees; fixed ones have a bolt), half-silvered splitters (each beam both passes through and reflects), coloured glass filters (only pass their own colour), stone pillars (block light) and crystals (absorb beams). A crystal's colour is the additive union of the beams that reach it, and it must exactly equal its required hue (red, green, blue, yellow = R+G, cyan = G+B, magenta = R+B, white = RGB). Later, Eye stones must stay unlit. The level is won when every crystal is correct. Beam tracing detects cycles with a visited set of cell+direction. Generation is reverse construction: choose crystal cells and their hues, then for each required colour random-walk a path back from the crystal to an edge emitter, placing a mirror at each turn and avoiding cells already used. The result is forward-simulated to validate it, and rejected on any mismatch, with retries using seed+attempt. Rotation levels then scramble a subset of mirrors; placement levels move some mirrors into a tray and add 1-2 decoy pieces. Any configuration that satisfies all crystals wins. Par is the number of changes from the scramble, and stars are given for meeting par.
games.controls: One thumb: tap a mirror to rotate it. In placement levels, drag mirrors from the bottom tray onto empty tiles (lifted 48px above the finger with a beam preview) and drag them off to return them. Keyboard: arrows move a cursor and Space rotates.
games.progression: Levels 1-8: rotation only, one colour. Levels 9-16: two colours mixing. Levels 17-24: splitters. Levels 25-32: tray placement. Levels 33-40: filters. Levels 41-50: white light and Eye stones. Level 51 onward is endless procedural with mixed elements. Grid fill, crystal count (1 to 5) and path length rise steadily. The run is saved, and progress shows 'Court 18'. Best = courts solved.
games.art: A moonlit tiled courtyard seen from above. A pre-rendered geometric eight-point-star tile floor in deep teal (#0e3b43 and #12505a) with cream grout (#d9cbb0 at low alpha) is crossed by arch shadows cast from a moon at the top right. Stone pillars and planters of dark-leaved citrus with tiny orange fruit form the obstacles, and a small fountain basin ripples in a corner. Brass mirrors (#c9a24a) sit on round stands with rim highlights and cast short shadows. Emitters are brass lenses set in the courtyard wall, each with a coloured glass disc. Beams are drawn additively (globalCompositeOperation 'lighter') as a wide soft glow plus a white-hot core, in red #ff3b3b, green #3bff6e and blue #3b7bff, and overlaps visibly mix to yellow, cyan and white. Dust motes drift in the beams. Crystals are faceted gems that fill with their received colour, with a small ring showing the target hue. HUD: a brass filigree arch across the top with gem sockets that fill as crystals are satisfied, and moves engraved on a brass coin. The menu shell is brass and teal tile. Light mode is a dawn courtyard: sandstone (#e8d6b5), pale aqua tiles, and beams drawn with saturated cores plus darker outlines so they read on light ground.
games.audio: Music: a 96 bpm loop of plucked-string arpeggios (Karplus-Strong) over a sustained drone and a soft frame-drum pulse (low sine thump plus noise slap), in a modal scale. SFX: a mirror turn is a brass clack with a short ratchet. When a beam lands on a crystal, a glass-hum tone plays for its colour (R = C, G = E, B = G), so mixed hues sound as chords. A wrong colour makes a gentle dissonant buzz, and solving a level gives a glass-harmonica sweep.
juice: Mirrors rotate with an ease-out overshoot and throw a shower of sparks where the beam deflects
Beams grow out at about 60 tiles per second instead of snapping, so you see the light travel
A correct crystal blooms, slowly spins and emits light rays, with a haptic tick
A wrong crystal flickers and shakes with the dissonant hum
On solve every beam flares white for a moment, the fountain sparkles and petals drift across
games.teach: Level 1 has one lens emitter, one mirror facing the wrong way and one crystal. The mirror pulses and a ghost hand taps it once. In level 9, a yellow crystal already receives red and only needs green, which teaches mixing by sight.
games.scenes: Art: the courtyard with three coloured beams crossing, a white crystal blooming and dust in the light, with no HUD. Shot1: Level 1 with the filigree HUD and ghost tap. Shot2: Level 30 placement, with the tray of mirrors, splitters, two mixed crystals lit and one wrong.
games.feasibility: Grid beam tracing is simple and deterministic. Additive canvas compositing is cheap at this size. The reverse-path generator with forward validation avoids needing a general solver. Beam glow should be pre-rendered per frame only when something changes, and nothing else redraws. Test hook ?debug: __game.start(level), .rotate(x, y), .place(x, y, kind), .solution(), .state(), .forfeit() (runEnd 'restart'). Estimated 1700-2300 lines.

games.title: Null Puck
games.pitch: Zero-g air hockey for two on one phone, or a solo tour of alien rinks with gravity wells, portals and drifting rocks.
games.hook: You drag your mallet, smack a glowing puck, and it curves around a little gravity well and rockets into the alien's goal while the rink flashes. It plays instantly like air hockey, then every arena bends it.
games.loop: TWO PLAYERS is the headline mode: lay the phone flat on a table between two people; each owns a half, each mallet follows its own pointer, and the score reads upright for both (each player's numbers face them). SOLO is a tour of rinks against alien champions. Top-down rink in portrait, goals at the top and bottom. Drag to move your mallet, which follows your thumb with an offset of 50 px toward the centre line so it is never hidden, limited to your half; its velocity is taken from the drag, so swinging through the puck hits harder. Physics: circle-vs-circle with mallet velocity transfer, a nearly frictionless puck with a speed cap, wall bounces, 4 substeps per frame so there is no tunnelling. A goal is scored when the puck crosses a goal mouth. First to 7 wins. The solo AI predicts the puck path with wall reflections and decides to defend (stay between puck and goal), attack (strike when the puck is slow on its side) or bank-shot, with reaction delay and aim noise by champion. Each arena adds one zero-g twist that both sides deal with: a central gravity well that curves the puck, a pair of portals that teleport it, drifting asteroids that act as moving bumpers, a rink rim that rotates (deflections spin the puck along the wall), magnetic lanes that push the puck sideways, or a 'split' charge (power shot) that fills when you hit fast and lets the next shot duplicate the puck for a few seconds.
games.controls: One thumb per player: drag to move your mallet (it rides 50 px ahead of your thumb toward the centre line). In two-player mode each half tracks its own pointer independently. Keyboard (solo): arrows or WASD move the mallet; Shift for a dash.
games.progression: Solo is a tour of rinks on a station map: 8 alien champions, each a different species and play style living in its own arena, and beating a champion unlocks the next rink. Blip (a jelly that defends lazily) on a plain ring; Grav-Monk (calm, banks shots) around a gravity well; Twin Kix (a two-headed sprinter) with portals; Rok (a rock creature who rams) in an asteroid field; Vortessa (tricky curves) on a spinning rim; Pulse Eel (fast) with magnetic lanes; Hive (strikes in bursts) where the split charge is enabled; and the Warden in a final arena mixing two twists. Losing a match ends the run (reason 'lose'), but rinks stay unlocked, so the next run can start at any rink you have reached. Every twist a champion has shown can be toggled on in two-player mode. Unlocked rinks and the tour score are saved between visits (progress pct = rinks / 8). Score = goals scored x 100 + win bonuses + bank and comeback bonuses; after the Warden the tour loops with faster AI. Best score is kept.
games.art: An orbital arena under a frosted glass dome on a space station, lit warm from inside. Palette: frosted dome glass (#cfe0e8 at low alpha with frost crystals at its edges), warm station interior light (#ffc98a lamps, #3a2a24 copper-brown deck), a deep blue-grey rink surface (#1c2a3a) with pale lines (#e8f0f4), your glow lime #B6FF3B, the opponent's magenta #FF2E88 (in two-player mode, lime and magenta), and a white-hot puck with a coloured trail of whoever hit it last. Layers: through the frosted dome, a soft-focus starfield and a huge slowly rotating planet (gradient sphere, banded clouds, soft halo); the dome struts in brushed copper with warm lamp reflections; the rink surface with a fine hexagonal grid that ripples outward where the puck hits; arena features drawn in code (a gravity well as a swirling dimple of rings, portals as rotating rings with an inner gradient, asteroids with craters). In solo the champion is drawn large above their goal as an animated alien bust (shapes, blinking eyes, reactions to goals). HUD: big score numerals at each goal, each set facing its own player, as glowing seven-segment glyphs, and the split charge as a ring around your mallet. Shell theme: station lounge, brushed copper and frosted dome glass (no neon, which belongs to Ringbreak).
games.audio: Music: driving synthwave at 118 BPM - gated saw chords, arpeggiated bass, punchy drum machine; each arena transposes the key and changes the lead patch, and the music gets a filter sweep at match point. SFX: mallet hit (punchy square blip, pitch by speed), wall bounce (glassy ping), gravity hum (low sine that rises when the puck is near the well), portal warp (pitch-bend whoosh), asteroid thunk, goal (big bass drop plus siren-like rising tone), match win (triumphant arpeggio), alien voice blips when the champion reacts (formant chirps).
juice: Goal: the rink flashes in the scorer's colour, screen shake 6px, hit-stop 8 frames, the alien bust reacts (cheers or sulks)
Hard hit: the grid ripples outward from the impact and sparks fly from the mallet
Gravity well slingshot: the puck trail bends in a glowing arc that lingers
Portal: the puck shrinks into one ring and pops out of the other with a burst of particles
Match point: the music filters down, the dome lights dim to a spotlight on the rink
Split shot: the puck cracks into two with a flash and both glow with your colour
games.teach: The title screen shows a live AI vs AI rally. Choosing two players shows two ghost thumbs, one on each half. The first solo match against Blip starts with a ghost thumb dragging the mallet into the puck, and Blip plays slowly for the first 2 goals. Each new arena twist gets a 2-second demo of the puck reacting to it before the faceoff (no text).
games.scenes: art: the puck slingshotting around a gravity well with a glowing lime trail, Grav-Monk's bust above, the big planet softened behind the frosted dome and warm copper lamps, no HUD. shot1: a two-player rally on the portal arena with both scores facing their players. shot2: a goal flash with sparks and the alien reacting on the asteroid arena.
games.feasibility: Risks: AI quality and puck physics. Mitigation: air hockey physics is just circles and lines; arena twists are each a single force or rule applied to the puck (well force, teleport, moving circle bumpers, tangential rim velocity, constant lane force), all deterministic. AI is a small state machine with prediction by stepping the same physics forward 1 s. Two-player input is two pointer ids mapped to halves, which Playwright can drive with two touches. Test hook: Arcade.test start() starts the tour, lose() forfeits the current match, and ?debug setAI('none') or forcePuck(x,y,vx,vy) let test.cjs check goals, match end at 7, rink unlocks and that the AI always returns the puck. Planet and dome pre-rendered.

games.title: Ringbreak
games.pitch: Spin twin shields around your tiny world and smash the asteroid belt closing in.
games.hook: The ball is already moving when you press Play. Asteroids crack into glowing shards on the first rebound, and holding one thumb whips both shields around the planet in a satisfying neon smear. It reads as breakout at once, but it is round and nothing else plays like it.
games.loop: A tiny ocean planet sits at the centre of a circular arena (planet r≈0.07W, shield orbit r≈0.2W, force-field rim r≈0.47W). Two shield arcs, each ~42°, sit exactly opposite each other on the shield orbit and turn together. A plasma ball bounces between the shields and the outer force-field rim. Between them are rings of asteroid chunks, which are circles drawn as faceted rocks. Where the ball hits a shield sets the outgoing angle, like the English on a breakout paddle. If the ball crosses the shield orbit inward without touching a shield, it hits the planet and you lose one of 3 moons. Every 20 s the belt tightens: all brick rings creep 6 px inward, shown by a dashed rim gauge filling. A brick reaching the shield orbit crushes it and ends the run. Clearing every brick finishes the 'system': the belt resets outward and a new seeded layout spawns. Brick types: rock (1 hit), ore (2-3 hits, vein colour shows HP), volatile (explodes neighbours), ice (the ball passes through and slows down), and rotating rings (whole rings orbit slowly, alternating direction). Destroyed bricks sometimes drop capsules that drift inward. Catch one with a shield for Split (3 balls), Wide (arcs grow to 70°), Pierce (8 s), Magnet (ball sticks, release by tapping both sides) or Third Shield (adds an arc at 90°). Score: 10 per brick × chain (bricks hit without touching a shield), plus a system-clear bonus scaled by time and moons kept.
games.controls: Two thumbs: hold the left half of the screen to move the lower shield left, hold the right half to move it right. The upper shield mirrors it. Tap both halves together to launch or release a magnetised ball. Keyboard: Left/Right or A/D to spin, Space to launch. The lower shield is drawn brighter as the reference, and the touch zones sit below the arena so thumbs never cover play.
games.progression: System 1 is a single slow ring with no rotation, and the belt timer starts at 30 s. Each system adds one rule from a seeded table: more rings, ore, rotating rings, volatile clusters, spirals, ice. Ball speed rises 4% per system up to a cap. The belt timer shortens to 14 s. Every 5th system is a 'core' layout: a dense armoured asteroid in one quadrant that has to be chipped to its glowing heart for a big bonus. The palette shifts per system (magenta grid, teal ion storm, amber dust, crimson flare), so long runs look different. The best system reached is shown on the title.
games.art: Deep space in a neon shell. Background: a pre-rendered radial gradient #0B0623 → #2A0F4F, a faint neon polar grid of rings and spokes centred on the arena (#FF3EA5 magenta and #3CF2FF cyan lines at 8-14% alpha, baked once to an offscreen canvas) instead of any nebula, three parallax starfields rotating slowly around the arena centre at different rates, and a distant gas-giant crescent (#7A3FD1 with a #FFB3E6 rim) in a corner. The planet is an ocean world #2BC4B4 with a cloud swirl band and an additive atmosphere glow. Bricks are faceted polygons in basalt #6B4E71 with bevel highlights. Ore veins glow gold #FFC94A, rose #FF5E7E or white by HP, volatile bricks pulse orange #FF8A3D and ice bricks are translucent #BDF4FF. Shields are cyan neon arcs (#3CF2FF core, wide additive blur) with a heat flare where the ball hits. The ball is a white-hot plasma dot with a fading comet trail. The force-field rim is a faint hexagonal lattice that ripples where struck. HUD: the score sits in thin Unbounded type inside a curved bracket above the arena. Lives are 3 small moons orbiting the planet, and the belt timer is the dashed rim gauge itself, so there are no pills or panels. Shell theme: neon (cyan tubes on translucent black); no other game in the catalogue uses a neon shell.
games.audio: Music: a driving 128 bpm synthwave loop in A minor on the sequencer: pulse bass, saw arpeggio and a gated noise snare. A layer adds when the belt is under 30% from crushing. SFX: shield hit (short square blip, pitch up with chain), brick crack (noise burst + low sine thump), ore chip (metallic FM ting), volatile boom, capsule catch (rising arpeggio), moon lost (descending sweep + rumble), belt creep (deep grind), system clear (major fanfare arpeggio).
juice: Chain counter pitch-shifts the brick crack upward, and at 10+ the ball trail turns gold
Volatile bricks chain-explode with a 60 ms hit-stop and radial shockwave ring
Belt creep: the whole ring shudders inward with a low rumble and a screen pulse, telegraphed by the rim gauge flashing
Losing a moon: slow-mo 0.3 s, the moon cracks into shards that spiral into the planet, camera shake
System clear: remaining shards spiral into the sun-glow, the planet's clouds swirl and the score counts up with ticks
games.teach: On the title, an attract demo shows the shields auto-tracking the ball. When play starts, two glowing thumb ghosts pulse on the left and right zones with arrows, and the first ball launches slowly straight toward the lower shield. The first system has no hazards, so the player learns spin-to-catch in 3 seconds.
games.scenes: art: seed 7, system 3 mid-play with no HUD. Two balls (Split active), a volatile chain exploding on the upper right, a rotating ore ring and the neon grid behind. shot1: seed 3, system 1 at 6 s with HUD, the ball rebounding off the lower shield, bricks half cleared, moons visible. shot2: seed 9, a scripted 'core' system with Pierce active, the ball tearing through the armoured core at a 14 chain, gold trail, shockwave mid-frame.
games.feasibility: Low-medium risk. All collisions are circle-circle (ball vs bricks) or radial (ball crossing the shield orbit: compare the angle to the arc span, then reflect about the radial normal plus an offset term). Run 4 substeps per fixed tick and clamp ball speed so it moves less than its radius per substep. Bricks are pre-rendered once per type to small offscreen canvases; rotating rings just add an angle. Layouts come from a seeded generator (rings defined by radius, count, type mix and rotation speed) with a rule that the first ring always leaves a gap. Test hook: start() begins system 1, lose() removes all moons, and state() exposes system, moons, bricksLeft and ball positions. test.cjs can run a bot that sets the shield angle to the predicted ball crossing angle and assert that a system clears and that belt crush ends the run. The only real tuning risk is control feel: angular speed should ramp from about 3 to 7 rad/s over 150 ms of holding.

games.title: Flailstar
games.pitch: Tow an asteroid on a chain and whip it through raider drones.
games.hook: You move the tug and the rock lags behind, swings wide and smashes a drone into shards with a crunch and a freeze-frame. The first big swing feels like a wrecking ball and you want to do it again at once.
games.loop: Your tug flies toward your finger. A 10-node verlet tether drags a rock (the mace) that swings with real momentum. Mace hits only count above 220 px/s, and damage scales with speed times mass; above the kill threshold the mace and chain glow hot white-orange, which tells you when a swing is lethal. Tap with a second finger (or double-tap) to cut the tether: the mace flies off as a projectile on its momentum. Then fly within 40px of any floating rock to hook a new one. Rocks: pebble (light, fast, low damage), boulder (heavy, slow, crushes), ice (shatters into 5 shards that keep flying), ore (explodes on impact, area kill, single use). Raiders: gnats (swarms, 1 hit), shields (front shield, so hit from the side or behind), turrets bolted to drifting rocks, lancers (draw a red line, then dash at your tug), harpooners (fire at your chain; a hit cuts it). Your tug has 3 hull pips, and raider contact or fire costs one. The arena is the screen, edged by a slow-rotating debris ring with soft walls.
games.controls: One thumb drag (tug follows with an offset above the thumb). Second-thumb tap or a quick double-tap releases the mace. Keyboard: arrows to fly, Space to release.
games.progression: Endless waves from seed. Every 4th wave brings an Anchor boss: a raider station inside a rotating armour ring with 2-3 gaps, so you have to whip the mace through a gap at speed to hit the core. Rock types unlock by wave (ice at 3, ore at 6). Multi-kills in one swing give combo stars, and 'Bowled' (5 in one swing) is the brag moment: it stamps BOWLED across the screen as a rock-cut seal and saves a separate best (most kills in one swing), shown on the title as its own brag stat. Enemy mixes rotate so a wave asks for a heavy boulder or quick pebbles. Best score and best single swing are saved separately.
games.art: A cold, bright comet field: a plum-black base (#1b1030) crossed by a huge luminous comet tail diagonally (#7ee8fa to #eec0c6 gradient with drifting ice-crystal sparkles) and drifting violet dust lanes. A small blue-white star at top-left lights everything, so every rock is a shaded sphere (radial gradient, crescent shadow, 2-4 crater ellipses) with a crisp rim. The tug is chunky and tugboat-shaped in safety-yellow (#ffcc33) with a cyan thruster. Raiders are angular crimson and black (#c1121f, #1a0a0f) with orange engine dots. The tether is a braided chain that heats from white to orange to white-hot with speed. HUD is minimal and diegetic: 3 ice-crystal hull pips orbit the tug, the score sits in huge translucent numerals at the top, and a thin speed arc around the mace fills to the kill threshold. Shell theme: chipped ice-rock slabs with chain-link borders and Unbounded numerals cut into the stone.
games.audio: Half-time drum-and-bass at 170 BPM: sub bass, triangle/square bell arps in Dorian, crunchy noise snare. SFX: a continuous whoosh (filtered noise whose cutoff and volume follow mace speed), a deep crunch on hit (sine thump plus noise), a glassy shatter for ice, a boom for ore, a twang when the chain is cut, a creak at full tension.
juice: Hitstop scaled to impact (30-120ms) and shake on boulder kills
Mace and chain heat up visibly and leave an ember trail when lethal
Debris fragments and ice shards with spin that fade into the comet glow
Three or more kills in one swing play 0.3 s of slow motion with a combo star burst; five or more slams a BOWLED stone seal onto the screen with a crunch
Chain snap from a harpoon whips the loose links around with a twang
games.teach: A ghost hand drags in a circle and the rock follows; three idle gnats float in range. The first swing almost certainly kills one. A one-line hint 'Swing it fast. Glowing = deadly.' appears until the first kill. Release is introduced at wave 2 with a pulsing ice rock and a two-finger hint icon.
games.scenes: art: the tug mid-swing with a white-hot boulder on the chain smashing through three crimson raiders, the comet tail behind, no HUD (this is the card art). shot1: wave 2, chain glowing, gnats bursting, with the speed arc visible. shot2: an Anchor boss with its rotating armour ring and the mace whipping through a gap.
games.feasibility: Medium risk, mostly in game feel. The verlet chain (10 nodes, 6 constraint iterations, fixed timestep at 120 Hz) is cheap and stable. Rocks and enemies are circles with no rigid-body rotation. Tuning constants (tug accel, chain length, mace mass) must be exposed in one object and tuned early; spec: the ship max speed is about 420 px/s and the mace can reach about 900 px/s on a full swing. The boss ring is an arc collision check. Debug hook: window.__game {start(seed), step(ms), lose(), setRock(type), state()}, and the seeded waves are deterministic under step().

games.title: Saltchart
games.pitch: Sail by the wind between islands. Match torn treasure maps to coasts and dig for gold.
games.hook: A big brass arrow shows the wind. Swing your bow across it and the sails snap full with a whump, the hull heels and spray flies, so the speed feels earned. Within seconds you spot an island whose coastline matches the torn scrap of map in your corner.
games.loop: A seeded archipelago of about 12 islands on a 4x4-screen sea, top-down and north-up, with the camera following the ship. WIND: a global direction that drifts slowly, plus gusts shown as streaks on the water. Ship speed follows a points-of-sail curve: 0.25 in the no-go zone (within 40 degrees of the wind, so never fully stalled), peaking at 100 degrees (beam reach), and 0.8 running downwind. Sails auto-trim. STEER: drag anywhere, and the bow turns toward the drag direction from the ship at a fixed turn rate. THE MAP: you carry a torn parchment fragment drawn from the target island's actual polygon. It shows part of the coastline silhouette, 1 to 3 landmark pictograms (palm, rock arch, skull rock, lighthouse, waterfall) and a red X. Find the island whose silhouette and landmarks match (landmarks appear when you are within a screen). When you are close to the right island, the fragment wiggles. ANCHOR by tapping the anchor button within 80px of a beach. The view zooms into a top-down beach scene of the same island, where one tap on the spot that matches the X relative to the landmarks digs it (two taps in all, counting the anchor), so the voyage stays the focus. A chest gives coins and the next map, or an upgrade. A wrong spot turns up a crab and the X wiggles as a hint. CARRYING treasure, sail it back to the home port to bank it. HAZARDS: reefs (lighter shallow patches that cost a hull plank), drifting storm cells (swirling wind and telegraphed lightning) and, from map 2, a navy cutter that chases ships carrying treasure, sails by the same wind rules and can be shaken by sailing closer to the wind than it can. Hull 3 planks; the run ends when the hull sinks. Banked coins = score.
games.controls: One thumb. Drag anywhere to set the heading (a ghost bow line follows your finger). Tap the anchor button (60px, bottom-right) near a beach. Tap the map in the corner to enlarge it. On the beach, tap the spot to dig it. Keyboard: Left/Right turn, Space anchor/dig, M map.
games.progression: Maps get harder by tier: tier 1 shows the whole coast plus landmarks; tier 2 shows half the coast; tier 3 is rotated (with a compass rose on the map so you must reorient); tier 4 shows only landmarks in sequence; tier 5 hides islands in fog banks so you navigate by chart. Upgrades from chests: jib (no-go 40 to 32 degrees, which beats the navy), copper hull (+1 plank), spyglass (landmarks visible from further), a stern chaser cannon (one shot to slow the navy, cooldown) and a star compass (night voyages, steering by the stars). The sea chart fills in as you explore and persists through the run, so the world feels mapped by you. Later voyages add a sea serpent in deep water (telegraphed by circling bubbles). The save holds chart, upgrades, current map and hull.
games.art: World: a painterly tropical archipelago from above. Sea depth runs from #0e4d6b through #1d8a99 to shallows #6fd6c8, with a pre-rendered depth-blend around each island, sand #f0d9a0, jungle #3f8f5a with palm crowns drawn as radial fronds, and rocks #8a8f99. Animated foam lines ring each coast (offset outlines whose dash shifts), wave chevrons drift with the wind, soft cloud shadows slide across the sea, and seabirds wheel. The ship is a top-down sloop: a wooden hull with deck planks, cream sails that billow in proportion to speed and flip across on a tack, a wake of foam particles, and spray on the bow in gusts. Storms are dark swirls with rain streaks and lightning that briefly lights the sea white. The map UI is parchment #e9d8b0 with burnt noisy edges, ink #3b2a1a line art and a red wax X. HUD: a brass compass rose top-right with the wind arrow, the hull as rope-tied planks, coins as stacked doubloons, and the map scrap pinned with a dagger top-left. Shell theme: parchment and sea teal with rope borders, as on a captain's desk.
games.audio: Music: a shanty feel in 6/8 at 112bpm. A squeezebox (two detuned squares with tremolo), plucked bass and a hand drum. During a navy chase it moves to a minor key, 132bpm, with a snare roll. On the beach scene it drops to ukulele-like plucks and ocean-wash noise. SFX: sail snap (noise burst with a low thump), wood creaks, wave slap, gust whoosh, a reef scrape crunch, a deep dig thunk, a chest creak then a coin jingle cascade, a cannon boom with a splash, thunder rumble and gull cries.
juice: The sails visibly fill and the hull heels when you hit a good angle, with bow spray in gusts
The dig sprays sand, the chest bursts open and coins fountain into the HUD stack
Near the right island the map scrap wiggles and glows as its coastline draws itself in ink
A reef strike shakes the screen, splinters fly and a plank pops off the HUD
Lightning flashes the whole sea white for a frame, with the ship silhouetted
games.teach: The first map's island sits in view off the bow, so the first goal is visible. The wind arrow pulses, and a ghost hand drags the heading across the wind to show the sails filling. The first beach has the X already highlighted. The navy only appears from the second map. The pause menu's How to play is a pictorial wind-angle diagram. tutorial_complete is tracked on the first banked treasure.
games.scenes: art: the sloop heeled on a beam reach, sails full and spray at the bow, passing a palm-crowned island with a rock arch, a storm cell on the horizon and cloud shadows on turquoise shallows. No HUD. shot1: early voyage with the map scrap enlarged showing a coastline and X, the matching island ahead, and the compass rose. shot2: the beach dig scene with sand spraying, a chest popping and the navy cutter visible offshore on the minimap.
games.feasibility: Medium risk. Islands are seeded polar-noise polygons, and the same polygon draws the island, the map scrap (clipped and possibly rotated) and the zoomed beach, so matching is always correct by construction. Speed is a one-function polar curve. The navy AI steers toward the player with the same polar curve (plus simple reef avoidance). The main risks are dull sailing and opaque matching, countered by a small world (4x4 screens), strong gusts, the proximity wiggle and landmark pictograms. Test hook: window.__game = { start(seed), steer(angle), step(frames), anchor(), dig(x, y), sinkShip() /* loses */, state() } exposing the target island and X so a bot can complete a voyage.

games.title: Apexline
games.pitch: Hold to drift through a rain-slick neon hill city. Survive the knockout: last place is out every lap.
games.hook: The car is already rolling on a wet grid with three rivals when the lights go out. At the first corner you hold one side of the screen, the car snaps sideways throwing neon-coloured spray, and sparks under the tyres go blue then pink. You let go, the boost kicks with a camera punch, and you pass a rival just before the lap line, where the car in last place has its lights switched off in a shower of sparks.
games.loop: Every night is a new closed circuit built from a seed: 8-12 control points sorted by angle around a centre with radial jitter, a closed Catmull-Rom spline, rejected and reseeded if it self-intersects or a corner radius drops under the minimum. The car always accelerates. Holding the left or right half steers that way. A short hold (<0.25 s) or low speed is a grip turn. A longer hold above 60% speed starts a drift: grip drops, the slip angle grows and boost charge builds with drift time and angle (tier 1 at 0.6 s blue sparks, tier 2 at 1.4 s pink, tier 3 at 2.4 s white). Releasing fires 0.5 / 1.0 / 1.6 s of boost. Tyre walls line the whole circuit: hitting one bounces you and costs speed, never ends the race. Neon puddles cut grip (longer, riskier drifts). KNOCKOUT: each night is four cars over three laps, and at every lap line the car in last place is eliminated (its lights die and it pulls off). Lap 1 cuts 4 to 3, lap 2 cuts 3 to 2, and lap 3 is the duel lap, one on one. Being last at a lap line ends the run; winning the duel clears the night and the next night starts on a new circuit. Rivals follow offset racing lines with a speed profile from curvature, drift-boost on chosen corners and have personalities (a blocker, a late braker, a steady one), with mild rubber-banding of plus or minus 6%. Score = knockouts survived across all nights x 1000 + drift-chain score; best = most knockouts survived.
games.controls: Touch: hold the left or right half of the screen to steer (works with one thumb hopping sides or two thumbs). Drifting happens on its own on long holds at speed, and releasing fires the boost. Keyboard: Left/Right or A/D.
games.progression: Each night is a seeded circuit in one venue of the inland hill city, in order: an elevated motorway interchange (wide sweepers and flyover crossings), a tunnel of tiled lights (long curves, no puddles, echoing engines), a market street (narrow hairpins, awnings, heavy puddles), a multi-storey car-park spiral (tight descending corners), and a funicular-rail crossing (a level crossing where the funicular car passes on a telegraphed cycle). Then the venues remix with tighter tracks. Rival pace rises from 92% to 104% across nights, and rain gets heavier on duel laps. Surviving nights unlocks code-drawn liveries and two more car bodies (Grip: short drifts and strong steering; Slide: long drifts and big boosts). A daily seeded 'Tonight's circuit' time trial gives a reason to come back. The knockout pressure and the risk of a tier-3 drift keep 20+ minutes tense.
games.art: A rain-soaked neon hill city at 2 am, inland and terraced up a valley, seen from above with a chase camera that rotates so the car always points up, sitting at 70% screen height and zooming out with speed. Palette: indigo asphalt #0d1030, wet sheen #1c2350, neon magenta #ff3d8b, cyan #2de2e6, sodium amber #ffb347, tunnel-tile white #e8eef5 and concrete grey #3a3f52. Layers: asphalt with baked noise and painted red/white kerbs; puddle ellipses showing blurred, mirrored neon blobs; amber pools under street lamps (additive radial gradients); flyover pillars, terraced rooftops with vents and water tanks, and abstract neon signs (arrows, rings, chevrons, no text) throwing coloured light onto the road; screen-space rain streaks plus ripple rings in puddles. Cars are vector bodies with glassy windscreen gradients, additive headlight cones, red taillight trails that smear when drifting, and violet tyre smoke. An eliminated car's lights die and it fades to a dark silhouette at the roadside. HUD styled as neon tubes: a big italic position numeral that flickers when it changes, a cars-left row of four tube dots that go dark one by one, and a curved tube boost meter that fills blue, pink then white. Shell theme: wet neon signage, black enamel with a humming magenta tube border.
games.audio: Darkwave synth at 118 bpm in a minor key: detuned saw pads, gated snare, a 16th-note arpeggio, plus an extra lead layer on the duel lap. Sound effects: continuous engine (two detuned saws through a lowpass, pitched by speed), tyre squeal (filtered noise with a pitch wobble while drifting), three rising blips for the boost tiers, boost fire (whoosh plus a low thump), wall hit (crunch noise), overtake (bright two-note chime), elimination (a fizzing neon short-circuit), lap (soft bell), rain bed (bandpassed noise).
juice: Drift sparks change colour at each charge tier, with a matching tick sound
Releasing the boost kicks the camera zoom, draws streak lines and gives a light shake
An overtake makes the position numeral stutter like a failing neon tube, then lock in with a chime
Puddle hits spray droplets tinted by the nearest neon sign
On the duel lap the rain gets heavier and the music adds its lead layer
At each lap line the last car's lights die with a fizzing short-circuit and a cars-left dot goes dark; winning the duel floods the screen with neon raindrops
games.teach: Before each of the first three corners a glowing chevron 'hold zone' is painted on the asphalt, with a ghost thumb pressing the correct side. The boost meter pulses on release. The first night is a wide, easy layout with slow rivals. Track tutorial_complete after the player's first tier-2 boost.
games.scenes: art: top-down view of the player's car mid-drift on a wet flyover corner next to neon-lit terraces, a pink spark trail, two rivals behind, rain streaks and puddle reflections, no HUD. shot1: the start grid with the lights, four cars-left dots and the tube-style HUD. shot2: the duel lap in the tiled-light tunnel, one rival alongside, boost firing and two dark cars-left dots.
games.feasibility: Medium risk, mostly in how the car feels. Use an arcade model: the velocity vector lerps toward the heading by a grip factor, and drifting lowers grip and adds a yaw offset, with no tyre physics. Draw the track every frame by stroking the spline with its width under a rotated transform (cheap) instead of baking a huge canvas. Bake decor in 512 px chunks and draw only the visible ones. AI picks a lookahead target on its offset line, with no pathfinding. Track generation is seeded and deterministic, with reject-and-reseed. Test hook: Arcade.test {start, lose, state}; ?debug exposes window.__game { start(seed, night), setInput(side), bot(true), knockOut() /* eliminates the player at the next lap line */, endRun(), state() } so Playwright can play a night with the bot and force an elimination.

games.title: Tidewheel
games.pitch: Spin trios of rockpool creatures round a point. Match three to wash them away.
games.hook: The first tap spins three crabs and starfish with a stony click and a splash. A cluster pops into rising bubbles and the pool cascades, so you get a chain reaction within seconds without reading anything.
games.loop: Flat-top hex board, 7 columns x 8 rows (odd columns offset half a cell). It holds 4-6 creature types: crab, starfish, urchin, anemone, periwinkle and goby. Every interior vertex touches exactly 3 hexes. Pressing selects the nearest vertex and highlights its trio, and releasing rotates the trio 120 degrees clockwise. A short leftward drag on release rotates it anticlockwise instead. Each rotation costs 1 wave, whether or not it matches, and an unmatched rotation stays rotated so you can set up combos. After a rotation, every connected same-type group of 3 or more hexes (clusters, not just lines) clears. Columns fall straight down, new pieces enter from a seeded RNG stream, and cascades raise a multiplier (x2, x3...). Specials: a cluster of 4 leaves a Pearl, which clears its 6 neighbours when matched. A cluster of 5+ leaves a Whirlpool, which clears every piece of the type it is matched with. A ring of 6 identical pieces round one hex becomes a Moonshell bloom, which clears the three hex lines through that centre. Each level is a Tide with 1-3 goals, shown as creature icons with counts (e.g. 18 crabs, 10 urchins), and a wave budget. You win when the goals reach zero: leftover waves turn into whirls that hit random pieces for bonus score, and stars are awarded by waves left. You lose when waves run out. Obstacles from later tides: barnacle crust (a piece needs 2 matches to clear), rocks (fixed, so any trio containing a rock cannot rotate) and kelp tangle (the piece cannot move; a match adjacent to it frees it). The board can never deadlock because any trio can always rotate. The initial board is generated with no pre-existing matches.
games.controls: One thumb. Touch anywhere near the meeting point of three creatures and the trio highlights, and a magnified copy appears 60px above the finger so the thumb never hides it. Slide to change the trio. Release to spin clockwise; flick left before release to spin anticlockwise. Keyboard: arrows move a vertex cursor, X spins clockwise, Z spins anticlockwise, Esc pauses.
games.progression: Tides 1-3 use 4 types with generous budgets and teach basic clusters. Tide 4 introduces Pearls (guaranteed on the opening board), tide 8 Whirlpools, tide 12 barnacles, tide 16 rocks, tide 22 kelp, and tide 28 Moonshell rings as goals. After that, tides are procedural from the tide number: 5-6 types, a mix of obstacle densities, 1-3 goals whose counts grow about 6% per tide, and a budget from a formula tuned during development by a headless greedy bot in test.cjs (budget = bot median x 1.2 early, falling to x 1.05). Every 10th tide is a 'spring tide' with an extra-large board and a special-heavy refill. Stars per tide plus a total-stars best score keep it fresh, alongside steadily new obstacle mixes. The run (current tide and stars) is saved, and progress shows 'Tide 14'.
games.art: Looking straight down into a sunlit rockpool at golden hour. The board sits in a hex-cut basin of wet granite (#5b5650 to #8d867a) with glossy rim highlights and dark wet edges. The sand floor gradient (#e8cf9a to #c79a5b) shows under translucent water (teal #1f8a8a at 20%). An animated caustic network (a pre-rendered tileable wavy-cell texture in two layers scrolling in opposite directions, composited 'lighter' at 0.15) plays across both pieces and sand. Bladder-wrack kelp silhouettes (#5d6b2a) sway at the board edges, and a few pebbles and a crab claw peek in from the frame. The creatures are chunky vector stickers with a dark outline (#2b1d14), a top-left highlight and a 2px drop shadow onto the sand: crab #e2553d with stalk eyes that blink, starfish #f29a2e with dot texture, urchin #6b3fa0 with radial spines, anemone #ff7aa8 with tentacles that sway on sine, periwinkle #f1e3c6 with a spiral, goby #2f8fd8 with a fin flick. Each type also has a distinct silhouette for colour-blind play. HUD: a carved sandstone tablet at the top with the wave budget drawn as a row of foam curls that wash away one by one. Goals sit in three scallop-shell bowls with Unbounded numerals. There are no panels or pills. The menu shell is driftwood and rope-edged sandstone. Dark mode is a moonlit rockpool: deep teal #0b2a33, silver caustics, and anemones and pearls glowing with bioluminescent rims.
games.audio: Music: a lazy 92 bpm loop of steel-drum/marimba timbre (sine plus a fast-decay 2nd harmonic) over a soft shaker (high-passed noise) in C major pentatonic. A bass layer fades in during cascades x3 and above. SFX: rotation is a stone-grind click (short noise burst plus a low square blip), match pops are bubble blips whose pitch rises a scale step per cascade level, a Pearl burst is a glassy chime chord, a Whirlpool is a downward filtered-noise sweep, a Moonshell is a bell bloom, the win is a marimba run, and the loss is a gentle descending marimba with a wave wash.
juice: Trio rotation eases out with a slight overshoot and leaves a white splash ring and droplets at the vertex
Matched creatures squash, hop up and dissolve into rising bubbles that wobble to the surface
The cascade multiplier appears as foam text (x2, x3) that bubbles up and pops, with the screen shaking slightly at x4 and above
A Pearl detonation sends a ripple ring that visibly bends the caustic texture, plus a small shake and haptic
Goal icons bounce and their numbers count down; a completed goal shell flips over with a sparkle
The tide-complete finale turns each leftover foam curl into a whirl that zips to a random creature with a rising pitch
games.teach: Tide 1 opens with a guaranteed one-spin crab match. The three hexes wiggle and a ghost hand taps their meeting point; after one success the hand disappears and tutorial_complete fires. The highlight that appears on press shows exactly what will spin before you commit.
games.scenes: Art: a dense rockpool board mid-cascade with a Pearl burst ripple, caustics, kelp edges and bubbles, with no HUD. Shot1: Tide 1 showing the sandstone goal tablet, foam-curl budget, highlighted trio and ghost hand. Shot2: Tide 18 with barnacles and rocks, a Whirlpool clearing urchins and the x3 foam multiplier.
games.feasibility: The main risk is hex vertex math. Specify flat-top offset columns, a precomputed list of interior vertices each mapped to its 3 cells, and nearest-vertex picking by distance to precomputed vertex centres. Matching is a flood fill and gravity is per column, so both are simple. Everything is tweened and nothing uses physics. Refills use one seeded RNG stream per tide, so a replay with the same inputs is identical. Budgets are tuned with a greedy bot in test.cjs. Test hook ?debug: window.__game.start(tide), .rotate(vertexIndex, dir), .state(), .lose() (sets waves to 0 and triggers runEnd 'lose'). Estimated 1800-2400 lines.

games.title: Nose Bump
games.pitch: One-on-one beach volleyball as a seal. Bump, set and spike with your nose against cove rivals.
games.hook: Your round seal slides across the sand, hops, and bonks a beach ball over the net off its nose; the crab opponent scuttles and misses, and confetti shells pop. The physics is so simple and bouncy that the first rally is fun before you know the rules.
games.loop: Side view of a beach court with the net in the middle: you are the seal on the left, the rival on the right. The seal's body is a half-circle for collisions, the ball bounces off it with restitution plus the seal's own velocity, so moving into the ball pushes it. Ball: a light beach ball with gravity and gentle air drag. Rules: up to 3 touches per side (the seal can touch the ball 3 times alone, which allows a bump-set-spike); the ball touching sand on your side is a point to the opponent; rally scoring; circuit matches are best of 3 games to 5, win by 2 (cap 8), and two-player matches are first to 7, win by 2. Nose spike: if the ball hits the seal's nose tip while it is at the top of a jump, it is a fast spike with a speed trail. Blocks happen naturally when both jump at the net. The AI predicts where the ball will land, moves under it, and decides to bump, set or jump based on style.
games.controls: One thumb: drag left or right anywhere to move the seal toward your thumb's x, flick up (or tap with the second thumb) to jump. Two thumbs also work: left half drags, right half taps to jump. Keyboard: Left/Right to move, Up or Space to jump.
games.progression: A summer circuit of 6 beaches, each a short best-of-3 match against a local animal whose home weather is its advantage: a crab on the calm cove (very fast, scuttles sideways), a pelican on the windy headland (huge reach; the wind pushes the ball sideways, shown by flags and spray, and it plays the wind), a walrus in the drizzle (the heavy ball suits its powerful hits), a puffin pair on the sunset dunes (they swap in after each point), an octopus on the night beach with glowing plankton (extra-long reach, clumsy), and the Elephant Seal champion on a rocky stage with a low net. Losing a match ends the circuit run (reason 'lose'); winning all six starts the next summer with stronger rivals. Circuit position and the match in progress are saved between visits (progress pct = beach / 6). Score = points won x 100 + aces and spikes bonuses + match bonuses. Same-device 2-player: two seals (or any two unlocked animals), each player owning one half of the screen: drag to move, flick or tap with a second finger to jump.
games.art: A sunny sandy cove with a red-striped lighthouse on the headland. Palette: sea teal #1FA2A6 to deep #0E5E73, sky #8FD3FF with soft cumulus, sand #F6D8AE with warm shadow #D9A97A, pebbles in grey-violets, the beach ball with coral #FF6B6B, sunshine #FFD23F and white stripes, the seal grey-blue #6B7A8F with a cream belly and speckles, a red bandana. Layers: sky gradient and clouds that drift; a far headland with the lighthouse and a slowly moving sailboat; animated sea waves (3 layers of sine bands with foam lines) washing up the shore; beach details like a sandcastle, a crab burrow, flags and a striped umbrella; the net drawn as a mesh that sags and wobbles when hit. Spectator gulls on posts react. Weather overlays per beach (wind spray, drizzle streaks, sunset tint, night with bioluminescent foam #7CF5FF). Characters are chunky, round and expressive, with blinking eyes and squash-and-stretch on jumps and landings. HUD: two buoys at the top corners floating on a little wave strip, each showing the score in a painted number, and touches left shown as 3 bubbles above the seal. Shell 'solid' with sandy panels, teal buttons and rounded chunky Unbounded headings.
games.audio: Music: sunny calypso-pop at 120 BPM - steel-drum-like FM lead, plucky ukulele (short Karplus-Strong strums), shaker and bongo noise percussion, a round bass; each rival gets a variation of the lead. SFX: seal bark on jump (formant chirp), ball bonk (rubbery pitched thump, higher for nose hits), spike whoosh, net shiver (soft rattle), sand landing (soft noise puff), point won (bright steel-drum arpeggio), point lost (comic descending honk), crowd of gulls squawking on long rallies, wave wash in the background.
juice: Nose spike: 5 frames of hit-stop, the ball streaks with a coral trail, the sand explodes with particles where it lands, screen shake 4px
Point: the scoring side's buoy bobs and its number flips, seashell confetti bursts
Long rally: after 6 hits the gulls start cheering and the music adds a percussion layer
Block at the net: both characters squash against each other, the net wobbles and a 'boing' plays
Match point: slow camera push-in toward the net, waves pause their foam flicker for a beat
Win: the seal does a belly-flop victory slide into the sea with a splash
games.teach: The title shows an AI vs AI rally. The first rally against the crab starts with a gentle serve to the seal and a ghost thumb dragging under the ball and flicking up. The crab plays at half speed for the first 2 points. Touch count bubbles teach the 3-touch rule visually.
games.scenes: art: the seal at the top of its jump nose-spiking the beach ball over the net with a coral trail, the crab ducking, lighthouse and sea behind, no HUD. shot1: mid-rally vs the pelican on the windy headland with buoys and touch bubbles. shot2: match point on the night beach with glowing foam and the win splash.
games.feasibility: Risks: AI that can return balls reliably, and jump-flick detection with one thumb. Mitigation: the physics is the classic circle-on-half-circle model with a fixed timestep, simple and stable; the AI predicts landing by stepping the ball physics forward, picks a target x offset to hit toward the net, and jumps when the ball's predicted height at its x is in range, with per-rival delay and error. Flick detection uses vertical pointer velocity over 80 ms; the second-thumb tap path is a fallback. Two-player input is two pointer ids mapped to halves. Test hook: Arcade.test start() starts the circuit, lose() forfeits, ?debug autoPlayer lets test.cjs play full matches bot vs AI and check scoring, the 3-touch rule, win by 2 and saved progress.

games.title: Hillfold
games.pitch: Drag a sheepdog to herd a skittish flock through gates and into the fold by sunset.
games.hook: Put a finger down and the collie races toward it. The sheep bolt away together like a living fluid, bleating, and you instantly feel the push-and-flow of herding. It is tactile and funny, and the first pen fills inside 20 seconds.
games.loop: Each field is a top-down hillside about 1.6 screens tall, with the camera following the dog. The dog runs toward a point 60 px above the touch, so the finger never hides it, at a capped speed with skid turns. Sheep are boids: separation, alignment, cohesion, grazing wander, wall avoidance, and a flee force within 110 px of the dog that grows with closeness. A quick tap without dragging is a bark: a scare pulse of 160 px radius on a 2 s cooldown, shown as a ring. The fold is a stone pen with a gate. A sheep fully inside counts as penned and gets a strong 'calm' state so it rarely leaves. When the quota is met, the gate swings shut and the field ends. Sunset is the timer, about 75 s, shown as a sun sliding along the ridge. Score: 100 per sheep, a time bonus, and a 'Tidy' bonus if every sheep is penned. Missing the quota (80% of the flock) by sunset costs one of 3 crooks, and losing all 3 ends the run. Field features: dry-stone walls with gaps, hedges, ponds and bogs that sheep avoid or slow in, a stubborn ram that faces the dog and charges (dog stunned 1 s, telegraphed by a head-lower), black sheep that are faster and drift away from the flock, and lambs that follow their ewe.
games.controls: One thumb: hold and drag to send the dog, quick tap to bark. Keyboard: arrows or WASD to run, Space to bark.
games.progression: A 24-field season built from seeded templates with hand-tuned rules, then endless 'Night trials'. Fields 1-3 are open grass with 6 sheep and a wide pen. Walls and gates arrive at 4, ponds and bogs at 6, the ram at 7. Sorting fields begin at 9: two pens, white sheep left and black sheep right. A wrong sheep in a pen doesn't count. Wind fields at 12 make the flock drift and leaves show the direction. Rain fields at 15 make the dog slide. Every weather field shows its effect in its first 2 seconds: the flock visibly leans downwind, or the dog skids on its opening turn, before the player has to act, which is what keeps 24 fields from feeling samey. A fox prowls the edges from 18 and scatters any sheep it nears; barking at it drives it off. Flocks grow from 6 to 30. A season completed adds a rosette to the title screen.
games.art: Watercolour uplands at golden hour, in a dry-stone and tweed shell. Grass #A7C957 and #6A994E with mowed stripe bands, shaded #386641 in hollows. Heather patches #9B6B9E, clover dots, and puddles reflecting the sky #CFE3EA. Dry-stone walls #B8B2A7 have dark joints #6F6A63 and moss tufts. Sheep are cream wool #F6F1E7 (layered circles with a soft outline) with charcoal #2B2B2B faces and legs; black sheep are #3A3A3A with grey faces. The collie is black and white with tan #C98B4B cheeks and a flagging tail. Long low-sun shadows #2E3A2A at 30%, a warm vignette #FFD8A8, and a moving light band of wind rippling across the grass. Butterflies, cloud shadows and swaying grass tufts are pre-rendered into a few frames. As sunset approaches the light warms toward #F4A261 and the shadows lengthen. HUD: a slate chalkboard at the top-left with tally marks for penned sheep, the sun-on-ridge timer strip at the top, and crooks shown as three small shepherd's crooks.
games.audio: Music: a gentle 90 bpm folk tune in G with a fiddle-like saw lead with vibrato, a harp arpeggio and a soft bodhran. A double-time layer comes in for the last 15 s. SFX: start whistle (two-tone sine), bark (noise + formant burst), bleats (FM with randomised pitch and vibrato, rate-limited), hoof patter (filtered clicks scaled by flock speed), gate clank, penned chime (pitch rises per sheep), ram snort, fox yip, sunset bell.
juice: Spooked sheep 'pronk' straight up with a wool puff when barked at
Each penned sheep pops a rising chime and a floating +100, and the tally board ticks a chalk mark
Gate swing-shut: slow camera ease over the full pen, the sheep settle and graze, and the score counts up
Dog skids kick up dust and grass particles, and its tail wag speed shows how fast you're penning
Ram charge: telegraphed head-lower, then a bonk with a small screen shake, cartoon stars over the dog, 60 ms hit-stop
games.teach: Field 1 starts with a ghost hand dragging the dog in a curve behind the flock, and the sheep drift into the open pen on their own. Then the player takes over with 6 sheep in an open field. A bark glyph appears on the third second if no tap has happened yet. The hint line reads 'Get behind them'.
games.scenes: art: seed 7 on a golden-hour sorting field, no HUD. The collie mid-sprint, a flock splitting around a wall gap toward two pens, long shadows and a wind ripple on the grass. shot1: seed 3 on field 2 at 6 s with HUD, the dog behind a loose flock approaching the gate, 2 penned, the sun mid-ridge. shot2: seed 9 at a field's end, the gate swinging shut on 18 penned sheep, a Tidy bonus count-up and dusk light.
games.feasibility: Medium risk, mostly tuning. Boids with N ≤ 30 run O(N²) per tick, which is fine. Walls are axis-aligned rects and segments with steering avoidance plus hard collision push-out. A corner-escape rule (a sheep pressed into a corner for over 1 s gets a tangential nudge) stops sheep getting stuck. Field generation uses seeded templates (pen position, wall rows with guaranteed gaps, obstacle scatter with clearance checks). Expose all tuning constants in one table. Run progress (field, crooks, score) is saved after each field and reported as Arcade.progress({label:'Field 7', pct: field/24*100}) while in the season, with no pct during Night trials. Test hook: lose() spends all crooks; state() exposes field, penned and sheep positions. test.cjs runs the classic herding bot (stay behind the flock centroid opposite the gate) and asserts it pens the quota on fields 1-5, which also proves the fields are solvable.

games.title: Snapvine
games.pitch: A chameleon in a dusk-lit baobab forest. Snap bugs with your tongue and fling beetles through the swarm.
games.hook: You tap a buzzing fly and a long pink tongue zips out and back with a gulp, and both eyes swivel to the next one. Then you snag a heavy beetle, swipe, and it ricochets off three bugs with rising bonks.
games.loop: The chameleon grips a swaying thorny vine in the lower third, and bugs fly in from the canopy. Tap anywhere: the tongue shoots toward that point (0.15 s out, 0.15 s back) and hits the first thing on the line. Small bugs (flies, moths, glowing beetle larvae) are eaten for points. Armoured beetles cannot be eaten; they stick to the tongue tip, and the next swipe flings the beetle along the swipe vector. It ricochets off walls and leaves up to 4 times, killing every bug it hits, and armoured swarms can only be cleared this way. Wasps home in on you and sting (3 lives). Tap the chameleon itself for camouflage: 4 s in which the colours wash into the leaves, wasps lose you and bugs drift close. It recharges by eating. Spiders drop on silk threads (snip the thread with the tongue and the spider falls on bugs below). Stink bugs: eating one dizzies you for 1 s, so read the stripes. A hawk's shadow passes over and you must camouflage in time or lose a life.
games.controls: One thumb: tap a target to snap; while holding a beetle, swipe in any direction to fling it; tap the chameleon for camouflage. Mouse works the same.
games.progression: The day moves through hours: morning (flies, beetles), noon (wasps, dragonflies with zig-zag flight), dusk (spiders, moths), night (glowing beetle larvae that drift up from the leaf litter and light the trunks; hawk passes are swapped for owls). Each hour is about 60 s and adds one bug type plus density. Combos come from chained ricochet kills and quick consecutive snaps. The chameleon's band colours shift with your combo heat (teal to orange to crimson). Best score and longest ricochet chain are saved.
games.art: A Madagascar-style dry forest at dusk: fat baobab trunks in soft rose-grey (#b98b7e) with bark creases, red laterite ground (#a4462b) far below, a lilac-to-apricot sky (#c9a3d6 to #f4b07a), spiny octopus-tree silhouettes (#4a3442) and thorny vines with small grey-green leaves (#7d8f6a) for the chameleon to grip. The backdrop is warm and desaturated on purpose, so the chameleon's bright bands pop: it is a panther chameleon with teal, orange and crimson bands (#1fb8a8, #ff8a3d, #e63946) that brighten with combo heat, a curled tail, a casque head and two independently swivelling turret eyes that track the nearest bugs. The tongue is a glossy pink elastic with a sticky bulb tip. Bugs are jewel-like: iridescent beetles with gradient sheen (green-violet), dusty moths, striped wasps. Night drops the sky to deep violet (#2a1d3a), and the light comes from glowing beetle larvae (#ffd36b) drifting among the trunks. HUD: dried-leaf badges hanging on thorny twigs (score carved into a leaf, lives as 3 speckled eggs, the camouflage meter as a leaf that fills with pattern). Shell theme: baobab bark and woven raffia.
games.audio: Tropical percussion groove at 96 BPM: woodblock clicks, shakers, kalimba-like triangle plucks with fast decay, a gentle marimba bass; ambient synth bird chirps between phrases; night swaps to a soft pad with cricket noise. SFX: tongue 'thwip' and 'slurp' return, gulp with a bulge, a sticky 'thock' grabbing a beetle, 'bonk' ricochets climbing the scale, a camouflage shimmer swell, wasp buzz approach panned by side, hawk cry tell.
juice: Tongue overshoots and wobbles back elastically; the throat bulges on gulp
Eyes swivel independently to track bugs (charm and a hint at targets)
Ricochet chain counter with escalating bonk pitches and spark bursts
Camouflage: a colour wave washes across the body into leaf pattern; the screen softly desaturates
Bugs pop into sparkles; wasp hits flash red with a small shake
games.teach: It opens with three slow flies hovering close, and a ghost finger taps one. The first beetle arrives alone above a cluster of armoured mites, and when you grab it a curved swipe arrow ghost appears. The camouflage tap is introduced when the first hawk shadow appears, with the chameleon pulsing. Only text: 'Tap to snap'.
games.scenes: art: the chameleon on a thorny vine with its tongue fully out catching a moth while a flung beetle ricochets through a swarm, baobabs against the lilac-apricot sky, no HUD. shot1: morning, the tongue mid-snap and the leaf HUD. shot2: night lit by glowing larvae, a ricochet chain of 4 and a spider dropping on silk.
games.feasibility: Low risk. The tongue is a timed raycast against circles, flings are a point with velocity reflecting off screen edges and leaf segments, and bugs are simple seeded flight paths (sine, zig-zag, homing). The chameleon is the art focus: a body path with band gradients, a tail spiral, a casque polygon and two eye turrets, pre-rendered where static. Tap versus swipe: a tap is under 12px of travel. Debug hook: window.__game {start(seed, hour), step(ms), tap(x,y), swipe(dx,dy), lose(), state()}.

games.title: Periapsis
games.pitch: Fly a survey probe through sunlit star systems. Burn to hold low orbits and scan every world.
games.hook: You start in orbit with a crisp amber instrument line drawn ahead of the probe. Hold one side and the predicted path bends live, and the moment it clicks into the dashed sample band around the next planet, the band lights and a tick sounds. Let go, coast, and the scanner sweeps the planet while you hold the orbit. It feels like flying a real mission within seconds.
games.loop: Each system is seeded: a star, 3 to 6 planets on deterministic circular rails, and some moons. Physics is softened inverse-square gravity from the star and planets, integrated at a fixed 120Hz. INPUT: holding the right half burns prograde (speed up, raise the orbit) and holding the left half burns retrograde (slow down, lower it). Burning uses fuel. A predicted trajectory 6 seconds ahead updates live and accounts for moving planets. It brightens where it enters a sample band and turns red where it hits a surface or the star. SAMPLING: target planets show a dashed sample band (a low-orbit ring). Stay inside it for 270 degrees of arc and the probe fires a scan beam, and the planet's card fills. Atmospheric worlds instead need a dip through a thin inner band without overheating (a heat gauge rises in the band and cools outside it). Inside a sample band a weak circularising assist helps you hold it, which keeps it forgiving. GRAVITY ASSISTS are an optional bonus, not the point: a flyby that changes speed by more than 20% shows an ASSIST stamp and refunds a sliver of fuel. RENDEZVOUS: sampling every target calls the mothership relay, which travels on its own orbit around the star. Match its orbit (stay inside its rendezvous ring, shown on the prediction, with near-zero relative speed) for 2 s to dock, upload the survey and jump to the next system. Matching an orbit is a different skill from holding a band, and it is each system's final exam. FAIL: hitting a planet, falling into the star, drifting past the system edge, or being out of fuel with no future encounter on the predicted path for 8s. Score = samples × system number + leftover fuel + assists.
games.controls: Two thumbs or one: hold the left half for retrograde and the right half for prograde, with throttle ramping up over 0.3s. Pinch is not needed: the camera auto-frames the probe plus the nearest body and target. Keyboard: Left/A retrograde, Right/D prograde.
games.progression: System 1 has two planets and one wide band. System 2 adds moons that perturb the path. 3: a gas giant with a swarm of tiny ice moonlets (moonlets chip the hull, and you get 2 hull points). 4: a binary star whose centres orbit each other. 5: an asteroid belt of drifting rocks. 6: comets on long ellipses that you can sample for fuel. 7: a dark planet that only shows on the trajectory line. From system 8 on, elements recombine with tighter fuel. An Atlas collects every planet type you sample (procedural look, glyph-coded names, no words). The save holds the current system, fuel, hull and Atlas, and the best score counts samples.
games.art: A sunlit system, no nebula anywhere: a deep ultramarine field (#0b1a4a) with sparse crisp stars, and a warm white-gold star (#fff1c8 core, #ffc76a glare) with a lens bloom and a soft anamorphic streak. Every planet is lit from the star with a sharp terminator, so day sides are bright and night sides near-black: banded gas giants, cratered rock worlds, ice moons with specular glints, lava worlds glowing on their night side. The probe is a gold-foil body with solar panels and a dish, with a small cyan engine plume. The trajectory is a crisp instrument overlay, not a glow: amber dashes (#ffb547) with tick marks for every second of flight, AP and PE markers at apoapsis and periapsis, sample bands as dashed white rings, danger segments in red (#ff5470) and the mothership's rendezvous ring as a pale green bracket. HUD: mission-control vector style. Thin 1px lines, corner brackets around the screen, a vertical segmented fuel bar on the right edge, a row of target-planet thumbnails across the top that fill with colour as you sample, and a heat arc around the probe that appears only when needed. Shell theme: orbital survey instrument (dark navy glass panel, amber tick-mark rules, a slowly turning periapsis dial on the title).
games.audio: Music: ambient arpeggiated synth at 84bpm. A slow saw pad through an LFO-swept lowpass, a minor 7th arpeggio that gains one voice per sample collected, and a soft kick that enters once the mothership is called. SFX: burn is filtered noise plus a low sine whose filter opens with throttle. Assist is a rising three-note chime. Sampling is a scanner sweep ('bweee-oo') then three blips. Docking is a soft clamp clunk, then a reverse-swell into a sub-bass drop as the jump starts. A ring-particle hit is a metallic tick. A crash is a bitcrushed noise burst. Overheating is a rising sine whine.
juice: Periapsis pass: time scales to 0.5 for 0.4 s at the lowest point of a flyby with a gentle camera push-in, and the PE marker flashes
The moment the predicted line enters a sample band, the band lights with a click and the trajectory pulses brighter
The sample beam sweeps scan lines across the planet's surface, and its thumbnail in the HUD fills with a colour flood
Rendezvous: the relative-speed readout counts down to zero, the docking clamps close with a clunk, and the stars stretch into streaks for the jump
A crash sends a shockwave ring, tumbling foil debris and a screen shake
games.teach: System 1 begins in a stable orbit. A ghost path shows that holding the right half raises the orbit into the outer planet's band, and a pulsing chevron sits on each screen half. The first sample needs a single burn of about 1 second. The first rendezvous is with a mothership on an orbit just outside your own, with its ring drawn large. Track tutorial_complete after the first sample.
games.scenes: art: a banded gas giant in the foreground with a razor-sharp terminator, the probe curving past on an amber instrument line with tick marks and AP/PE markers, the white-gold star glaring with lens bloom on deep ultramarine. No HUD. shot1: system 1 with the probe in orbit, the predicted path clicking into a sample band, and the HUD brackets and fuel bar. shot2: the rendezvous with the mothership relay, the relative-speed readout near zero and two thumbnails filled.
games.feasibility: Low to medium risk. Physics is about 40 lines. Prediction is 720 fixed steps per frame (6s at 120Hz) over at most 8 bodies, which is cheap. Planets on rails keep the simulation deterministic. Planet rendering uses pre-rendered sprites per planet at load (gradients, bands, craters), rotated with the terminator overlay drawn live. Rendezvous is a distance-plus-relative-speed check held for 2 s, which a scripted bot can hit. The main risk is orbital mechanics feeling opaque, handled by the always-on prediction, wide bands, the circularising assist and an auto-framing camera. Test hook: window.__game = { start(seed, system), thrust(-1|0|1), step(frames), crash() /* loses the run */, state() } so a bot can run a fixed burn script and assert a sample was taken.

games.title: Barnstorm
games.pitch: A red biplane air race in bright daylight: thread gold rings, knife-edge through arches and fly upside down under bridges.
games.hook: From behind a red biplane you rush low over turquoise water toward a gold ring. A thumb nudge threads it with a rising ding and a burst of sparkles, the next ring rings higher, and then a stone arch narrows ahead: the plane snaps onto its side, knife-edges through the gap with a whoosh and rolls level in a sunlit boost past a rival.
games.loop: An into-the-screen chase view in bright daylight. Each course is a seeded 3D spline over an island sea, about 2 minutes point to point. The plane rides the spline at speed v. You control its offset (u, w) in the course frame within a 40-unit corridor, with inertia and a visual bank, which keeps the flying readable and impossible to get lost in. Rings along the line give +6% speed each and stack into a chain of up to 5. Missing a ring resets the chain. Pylons at turns must be passed on the arrowed side, and the wrong side costs 2 s. KNIFE-EDGE: where the corridor narrows to a slot (stone arches, gaps between sea stacks), the plane rolls onto its side automatically as you enter, and lining up the slot is the skill; clean knife-edge passes add to the chain. INVERTED PASSES: bridges span parts of the course, and flying under one while holding the stick down flips the plane upside down for a bonus chain step and a crowd cheer. Sea stacks, bridge piers and gull flocks block parts of the corridor: a hit spins you and costs 40% speed. Forks offer under-the-bridge or over-the-headland routes. Five rival planes have seeded speed profiles and lines. SEASON TABLE: each season has 8 courses scored 10/7/5/3/2/1, plus 1 point for the longest chain of the race, and the table is shown between races. You win the season by clinching the title; the run ends (reason 'lose') the moment you are mathematically eliminated, too far behind the leader to catch up in the races left, so every race matters and a bad season can end early. Score = season points x 1000 + longest chain.
games.controls: One thumb: relative drag works as the stick (the thumb moves the plane; the plane sits at 40% screen height so the thumb in the lower half never covers it). Keyboard: arrows or WASD.
games.progression: Course themes per season: sea stacks, a fjord with stone bridges to fly under, a river canyon, a volcanic island with ash plumes, a cloud-bank course where fog hides the next ring until late, floating rock islands, and a final grand prix that mixes everything. Rings get closer and more offset, and wind gusts (visible streaks) push you sideways. Rivals get faster. Planes unlock per season (a monoplane racer that is fast but drifts, a seaplane that is steady, a triplane that is agile) along with liveries. The run is saved mid-season with the label 'Season 1 · Race 5'.
games.art: Bright midday adventure, the daylight opposite of Aurora Pass. Sky from cobalt #2f6fde to pale #bfe3ff at the horizon. Pre-rendered white cumulus billboards with soft lit tops and shaded bases, sorted by depth. The sea goes from turquoise #1fb3b0 near shore to deep #0b5d8f, with scrolling sun-glitter specks and white surf rings around islands. Islands are emerald #3fae5a with sand rims. Sea stacks and arches have striated rock bands and white gull specks. Stone bridges cross fjords on tall piers. Rings are glowing gold hoops trailing ribbons. Pylons are red and white striped with pennants. Distance fog blends everything toward the horizon tint. The plane is a red #d7263d biplane with cream wings, a spinning propeller blur disc and the pilot's scarf flapping, banking with your input. HUD styled as an art-deco air-race poster: brass circular gauges for speed and ring chain, the position as deco numerals in a sunburst badge, and a small season-table badge, in cream #f4e8c9, red and navy. Shell theme: a deco poster with sunburst rays and stepped borders.
games.audio: Brassy big-band swing at 140 bpm: square-wave brass stabs, walking bass, brushed snare. Sound effects: propeller drone (sawtooth with an amplitude wobble tied to speed), ring pass (a ding whose pitch climbs with the chain), full chain (short fanfare), pylon round (whoosh), wrong side (buzzer), gust (noise swell), crash spin (engine sputter), gull cries.
juice: A ring you fly through shatters into sparkles while speed lines flare and the chain gauge needle jumps
At a full chain of 5 the field of view widens with a sun flare and a fanfare
The horizon tilts as you bank
Knife-edge: the horizon snaps toward vertical, the wingtips skim the rock with a whoosh and puffs of rock dust, then the plane rolls level
An overtake flashes the rival plane's livery as it falls behind
At the finish your smoke trail draws a loop over the line while the season table slides in
games.teach: Course 1 starts with three rings straight ahead and a ghost thumb nudging gently, the second ring slightly offset. The first pylon has a huge arrow and a ghost swipe. Track tutorial_complete after the player's first 3-ring chain.
games.scenes: art: the red biplane knife-edging through a narrow stone arch between sea stacks with two rivals ahead, cobalt sky, white cumulus and turquoise sea, no HUD. shot1: the start over a fjord with six planes and the brass gauges. shot2: an inverted pass under a stone bridge with the ring chain at 4, position 2 and the season-table badge.
games.feasibility: Low to medium risk. No meshes: only 3D point projection, scaled billboards and 2D-drawn sprites, sorted by depth.
